Vladimir Vapnik y Alexey Chervonenkis de: Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis developed the theory from 1963 in Moscow, and for decades it was almost unknown outside the Soviet Union. The leap came when Vapnik emigrated to Bell Labs: in 1992, with Bernhard Boser and Isabelle Guyon, he published the kernel trick, and in 1995, with Corinna Cortes, the soft margin that allows invasions. That 1995 paper is titled simply Support-Vector Networks and is one of the most cited in the discipline. The theory Vapnik and Chervonenkis built to justify it tries to answer the underlying question of the whole block: why a model that gets right the examples it has seen should get right the ones it has not.
Y aquí llega la idea que hizo famoso a e: And here comes the idea that made this method famous. If you look carefully at how the problem of minimising $\Vert\vec w\Vert$ with those inequalities is solved, it turns out the data appear only in dot products $\vec x_i \cdot \vec x_j$. Nowhere is a single point needed: they always appear in pairs and multiplied.
Y cuando ni con núcleo se separa —o no i: And when not even a kernel separates — or it is not worth it — some points are allowed to invade the corridor by paying a penalty. A parameter decides how much each invasion is punished: with a very high penalty perfect separation is demanded and the boundary contorts; with a low penalty getting a few wrong is accepted in exchange for a wider corridor and a more sensible boundary. It is the same dilemma between memorising and generalising that runs through the block.
